summary: Adds incremental zone transfer to DNS, so a secondary server can fetch only what changed in a zone instead of copying the whole thing. This saves bandwidth and time when large zones change in small ways.

plainLanguage.summary: IXFR lets a secondary DNS server tell another server which version of a zone it has. The server can then send only the changes needed to catch up, with a full-zone transfer available as a fallback.

subtitle: How DNS servers transfer zone changes instead of sending a complete zone each time.

tldr.problem: A full DNS zone transfer sends the entire zone even when only a small part changed.
tldr.mechanism: An IXFR client sends its zone's SOA serial. The server returns ordered deletions and additions from that version to the current version, or sends a full transfer.
tldr.outcome: IXFR saves transfer work when the server retains useful change history. RFC 1995 updates RFC 1035 and is updated by RFC 9103.

today: RFC 1995 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1996. It updates RFC 1035 and is updated by RFC 9103.

sections.title: Why Incremental Zone Transfer Exists
sections.content:
DNS changes need to reach secondary name servers. AXFR transfers a complete zone, so it can send much more information than necessary when only a small part changed.

IXFR is an incremental transfer. The server requesting changes is the IXFR client; the server responding is the IXFR server.
sections.plainLanguage: IXFR sends zone changes without requiring a secondary server to copy the entire zone every time. It is useful when only part of the zone has changed.

sections.title: Requesting Changes
sections.content:
The IXFR query carries the SOA record for the client's current zone version. A server that has change history can send the differences needed to make that version current, or it may choose to send the whole zone.

If the client's serial is the same as or newer than the server's, the server replies with one SOA record. Queries may use UDP or TCP; if an incremental UDP response does not fit in one DNS packet, the server sends a single SOA record to prompt a TCP retry.
sections.plainLanguage: The client tells the server which version it has. The server sends changes when it can, and can fall back to the full zone or ask the client to retry over TCP.

sections.title: The Incremental Response
sections.content:
An IXFR query uses the normal DNS query format, with IXFR as its query type and the client's SOA in the authority section. An incremental response starts with the server's current SOA, followed by the client's older SOA.

Each difference sequence represents one serial change and lists removed records and added records. Sequences run from oldest to newest. The client should replace its old zone only after all differences have been processed successfully.
sections.plainLanguage: The response lists zone edits in order, starting from the client's version. The client keeps its old copy until it has applied every change successfully.

sections.title: History Retention and Condensation
sections.content:
A server may delete old zone versions at any time. The RFC recommends purging history when an incremental response would be longer than a full transfer; this limits the storage needed for the history to at most twice the current zone information.

A server may combine several difference sequences and discard intermediate versions. If the client later asks from a version the server no longer recognizes, the server should attempt a full transfer rather than return an error.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers do not have to keep every past change. If the needed history is missing or too large, the client can receive a full copy instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC does not attempt to fix existing DNS security problems. It states that IXFR is believed to introduce no additional security problems to the DNS protocol.

For UDP responses, the RFC recommends checksums. A cautious client that receives a UDP response with a zero checksum should ignore it and try TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: This specification does not add DNS security protections. It recommends checksums for UDP responses and describes a TCP retry for a zero-checksum response.
